The humble Late Domain Era mining laser is, in reality, a hyper-advanced, hyper-ruggedized, hyper-economical piece of technology, made so by the needs of the late-era Domain economy and its reliance on asteroid mining. 

Ubiquitous among civilian populations, these mining lasers were designed to be too weak to serve as weapons—not through software lockouts, but through the compactness of the underlying technology. Their small form factor limits how much they can be cooled before the laser is destroyed by its own power input. 

In the years 60–61 after the Collapse, the pirate lord Francis Drake held a short reign of terror with a new hack-job weapon. It used a hacked, small-form-factor mining laser powered by Domain-restricted chemical laser fuel in the form of sacrificial shells as ammunition. His weapon proliferated quickly, and although he was eventually defeated, his name remains immortalized in the colloquial name of the weapon type. In the hundred and fifty years since, the weapon type has remained popular due to its ability to deliver the utility of a beam weapon without requiring an energy weapon mount on a ship.

The production template that produces the modern Drake is itself a hack-job of a mining-probe launcher, heavily modified with the laser-focusing optics of a military-grade hull-boring laser and the cooling systems of a high-impulse-power fusion reactor, capable of holding back the tremendous surge of heat produced when the weapon fires.

The ammunition is a small-form-factor, Domain-era mining laser, hacked down to the least and most stripped-down version possible, then modified to be powered by a canister of Domain-restricted chemical laser fuel. The result is a compact, powerful laser shell.
